The woman had noticed someone following her and had already called the police; that call fell before the nine minutes the phone could reach back to. The killer hid until the right moment, then came to the door to stage the appearance of having just broken in. She dialed, believing she had returned to a time before the killer entered, and locked the front door — locking the man hidden inside in with her. Nine minutes later, the police, acting on the report that still existed, came — and the door she had locked now barred their way. The killer heard her turn the lock, knew the trap had worked, and stepped out of the wardrobe.
hints: Going back nine minutes does not erase the people who already existed at that time.
The killer had entered the flat before she ever saw him 'break in'.
At the moment she returned to, the killer was already hiding in the wardrobe; her locked door also stood between the arriving police and her.

title: The Nameless King
story: When the new king was crowned, his first command was to open the tombs of all the kings before him and grind their names off the gravestones. When the turn came to his father's tomb, he embraced the stone tablet himself. The mason chiseled off the last character — and the new king's crown dropped to the ground, his robe left empty.
answer: The royal line was bound by an ancient curse: as long as each dead king's full name remained written on some object in the world, his bloodline went on existing; erase the last place his name was written, and the descendants who carried it on would vanish with it. The new king knew the secret and wanted to destroy the ghosts of ancestors who refused to yield their power — but he wrongly assumed his own name in the royal genealogy was enough to keep him existing on his own. After the earlier tombs were effaced, nothing happened, because those ancestors' names had other copies in the genealogy. His father, to keep anyone from casting spells with his true name, had long since burned every other record and left only the tombstone. The last character was chiseled away — and the new king, his descendant, vanished with it.
hints: The royal line's existence depended on its ancestors' names surviving somewhere in the world.
The earlier ancestors' names had other copies elsewhere.
His father's tombstone held the last copy of the name; erasing it completely erased the new king, his descendant, too.

title: Selling Yesterday
story: Someone was buying memories at the mouth of the alley. I sold my yesterday; when I came to, the blood on my clothes had already dried. The buyer sat across from me, poured me a cup of tea, and said he could pay more. I asked what else he wanted to buy. He said, 'The part where you're seeing me right now.'
answer: The memory dealer can only take what a person has already lived through; he cannot change what happened. The day before, the man had stumbled onto the buyer committing a murder; wounded during the chase, he had blundered into the alley and sold that memory of terror to the very killer, now in disguise. The trade done, he forgot the pursuit and forgot why he was covered in blood. The buyer took off his disguise to examine the extracted memory, confirmed he had been seen, and realized the man had glimpsed his true face while awake. So he raised his price, trying to buy this meeting as well — so that the only living witness would never walk out of the transaction.
hints: The trade erased only the memory; his clothes and wounds still carried yesterday's traces.
The man who chased him yesterday is the buyer of today.
After buying the memory of the murder, the buyer showed his true face; now he had to buy this meeting too.

title: The Son Behind the Window
story: Every day I watch my son through a window. He never notices me, but still I watch him go to school, marry, and grow gray hair. Today he finally looked up and called me 'Mama'. I did not open the window — I did everything I could to drive him away.
answer: The mother had died young; her ghost stayed inside the window of the old house, kept alive by her son's memories. The living cannot see anyone inside that window — only when a person's life is ending, when the soul is about to leave the body, can they hear and see their own kin. The son lived on in the world for decades; the mother stayed exactly as she was at death. Today, critically ill, the son walked in a dream to the old house and saw her for the first time. She knew that once the window opened and he stepped in, he could never return to the body the doctors were still fighting to save, so she feigned fierceness and drove him out. The word she had waited half a lifetime to hear — 'Mama' — had become the word she most dreaded.
hints: The mother had died long ago; inside the window is where the dead linger.
That her son could see her meant he was close to death himself.
She refused to open the window so that her dying son would return to the body that could still be saved.

title: Unmute Yourself
story: A week after my friend vanished, he suddenly joined our game voice chat. He said he had gone off to clear his head, and laughed the way he always had. I asked him to turn on his mic. He went silent. A few seconds later he left the voice room — and when the police broke down the door, they didn't find him either.
answer: My friend was already dead. His killer held his account and played old recordings of his game chatter — 'gone off to clear my head' and other lines vague enough to deflect questions — to fake the appearance that he was alive. The voice the narrator heard came from audio shared into the room, while the friend's microphone icon had shown muted the whole time; and that laugh was exactly the one from an old livestream. That is why he asked the 'friend' to turn on his mic and say a phrase he made up on the spot. The killer could not do it, dropped offline, and fled. The police, who had been watching the login because of the missing-person case, traced it to an empty house and found only a player and an abandoned computer; the real friend had long since been elsewhere.
hints: Hearing a voice does not mean someone is speaking live.
The friend's mic status and that familiar laugh raised suspicion.
The killer was playing the missing man's old recordings and could not answer a question improvised on the spot.

title: The Last Seat
story: The ship was going down. My father gave the last place in the lifeboat to a stranger. But once the man climbed in, my father leapt into the water and strained to shove the boat back. The rescue ship in the distance had already spotted us, yet he shouted, 'Don't go there!'
answer: The fishing boat they sailed on had been sunk by pirates. The father gave the last place to a crewman who had climbed up out of the water, planning to hold on outside the boat until rescue. As the man came close, the father recognized the tattoo on his wrist — he was one of the pirates who had boarded earlier to kill, then fallen overboard by accident. The ship blazing with 'rescue' lights in the distance was the pirates' mother ship, waiting to collect its own. The stranger snatched the oars and urged everyone to row toward it, so the father swam to stop the lifeboat from going near, shoving it instead toward the lights where the honest fishermen gathered. The kindness of taking in a stranger had nearly delivered them all into the same hands twice.
hints: The man taken aboard had been part of the attack.
The distant lights were disguised as a rescue signal.
The 'rescued' man was a pirate steering the whole boatload of survivors toward his own ship.

title: The Last Page
story: My cellmate wrote a prison-break novel and begged me to publish it if I ever got out alive. He died the night before he was to act. I followed the route in his book and escaped the prison — but when I turned to the last page, I climbed back in.
answer: The cellmate was an engineer held in a military prison. He had discovered that a ventilation shaft led to the coast, so he wrote up his surveyed route as a novel and smuggled it past inspection. The narrator took the ending for fiction and, breaking out early, never finished the book. Only at the coast did he turn to the last page and find a row of gates marked with tide times: beyond the exit lay a culvert that the tide poured into, passable only on a set date at a set hour. He was a day early, the sea was already rising, and the narrow culvert was about to go under. He retreated along the book's return route, waited for the true window, and preserved the map that could carry the other prisoners out.
hints: The novel was a smuggled escape manual.
Beyond the route, the timing of the escape mattered just as much.
The exit ran through a culvert the tide would fill; a day early, he had to go back and wait for the ebb.

title: Sewn In
story: I dress the dead for a living. The woman who came in today was sewn into her clothes — cuffs and collar all locked shut with red thread. The family told me not to undo it; I snipped a stitch anyway. A small paper roll tumbled out from her collar.
answer: The woman had been abused to death by her husband. Sensing she might not live long, she had sewn a small paper roll — naming where her evidence was hidden — into the collar of the underclothes she wore most, hoping whoever prepared her body would find it. After killing her, the husband felt something hard under the fabric; not knowing what it was, and afraid that undressing her would expose the wounds, he stitched every opening shut with coarse red thread overnight, claiming the dead had a custom of never being undressed. The mortician saw the red thread pressed over bloodstains that had not even been cleaned, refused to comply, and picked out the stitches to find the paper roll. The location on the paper pointed to her old sewing machine, where she had hidden recordings and photographs of her injuries.
hints: The red thread had been sewn on hastily after her death.
The family feared anyone taking off her clothes.
She had sewn the hiding place of her evidence into her collar; her husband sealed the clothes shut, but still could not stop the mortician from finding it.

title: Take the Heavy One
story: When the monastery caught fire, the abbot would only allow us to save the lighter books. I picked up the thickest one, and he lunged at me, tore it from my arms, and hurled it into the flames. The spine split open and several gold teeth dropped out. The children in the cellar had not sung for three days.
answer: The monastery had secretly sheltered a group of refugees. After confiscating their valuables, the abbot handed the adults among them over to the occupying army for money and kept the children for forced labor. The children in the cellar noticed their parents missing, began refusing to sing in the choir, and were moved away and locked up by the abbot. He hid the valuables stripped from the dead — gold teeth among them — inside hollowed-out thick books. When resistance fighters came to search, he set the fire to destroy the evidence and ordered the young monks, who knew little, to save only the light books, fearing the hidden compartments would spill open if the heavy ones were moved. The narrator happened to seize the very book holding the loot; the abbot snatched it and threw it into the fire, the spine burned apart, and what the children's parents had left behind came to light. The children falling silent, the ban on heavy books, and the fire all belonged to the same cover-up.
hints: The abbot had hidden things inside the hollowed-out thick books.
The children in the cellar had come for shelter with their parents.
The abbot betrayed the children's parents, hid the gold teeth he had taken inside the book, and set the fire to destroy the evidence.

title: The Guide
story: When the lights went out in the cave, the guide had us walk with a hand on the shoulder of the person ahead. I was last in line, counting every turn we took. At the ninth turn I suddenly sat down on the ground and refused to move. The others kept urging me on; the guide stopped speaking.
answer: The guide worked for a tomb-raiding gang: on the surface he led tourists through the caves, but he meant to trap anyone who found the underground ruins deep inside and silence them. Afraid of getting lost, the narrator had memorized the route the guide described on the way in: back to the entrance took only eight forks. After the lights failed, the guide led them down a different looping side passage with nine turns, planning to slip away at the last stone gate and seal it behind him. The narrator also remembered a cold draft beside that ninth turn — the guide had said earlier it came from a maintenance shaft leading outside. He deliberately stopped and called out, keeping the whole group in the open space inside the gate, then grabbed the guide's jacket and would not let go, forcing him to lead everyone out through the maintenance shaft.
hints: He had memorized the route to the exit on the way in.
A ninth turn meant the group had left the route back.
The guide meant to lead them into a passage he could seal; the man at the back saw through the route and gripped him so he could not leave alone.

title: The Youngest Child
story: Every winter, the youngest child in the village must go and open the door for the mountain god. This year it was my little brother's turn. I hid with him in the cellar — and the villagers never came looking. At midnight my mother's labor pains began, and everyone outside knelt down together.
answer: The mountain god, sealed underground by the villagers' ancestors, could only have the youngest living person in the village push open the temple door for it. Each year the villagers sent their youngest child, trading a crack of the opening door for a warm winter; the child was taken by the god. The sister hid her brother precisely to stop the rite; but the clan elder knew the mother was near her time — the moment the newborn arrived, the brother would no longer be the youngest. The villagers kept watch outside the house, waiting to carry the baby up the mountain once it was born. Only when she heard the mother's cries did the sister understand why no one was in a hurry to search the cellar.
hints: What the mountain god demands is whoever is currently the youngest living person in the village.
The mother was about to give birth.
The villagers were waiting for the newborn to replace her brother as the offering — that is why they stopped hunting him.

title: The Truth Stone
story: My father held a stone and asked me, 'Have you ever killed anyone?' I said no, and the stone stayed silent. He let out a breath of relief. Then I saw the words 'don't drink' carved all over the back of my hand, and suddenly asked, 'Dad — just how much have you made me drink?'
answer: The lie-detecting stone can only tell whether the speaker is deliberately lying. The father ran his son for an organization of killers: each time he forced him through a killing job, he dosed him with a drug that wiped away the day's memory, then used the stone to check whether he still remembered. In flashes of lucidity, the son tried to leave warnings for the self he would be the next day, carving 'don't drink' where it would not easily rub away — the back of his hand. That day the drug had worked; he honestly believed he had never killed anyone, and the stone kept silent. The father was reassured — but reading the carvings layered one over another, the son saw the resistance left behind by his earlier selves.
hints: The stone detects deliberate lies; it cannot restore memories.
Before every check, the father made him drink the same drug.
He was forced to kill, then had the memory wiped; the carvings on the back of his hand were warnings his lucid self left for himself.

title: The Shadow Shop
story: I sold my shadow to pay for my mother's treatment. But when I got home, she pushed me out the door and gathered up the shadow on the ground, calling it her son. I stood outside all night. At dawn, the me inside the house finally came out.
answer: After buying a shadow, the shadow shop sends it home wearing the seller's face and memories, to replace the seller bit by bit. Only kin can tell the two apart: if the family acknowledges the real person, the shadow disperses; if they acknowledge the shadow, the real person can never enter that home again. The mother had struck her own bargain with the shopkeeper long before: she wanted back her eldest son, dead years ago, and the price was her younger son's shadow. The news of her grave illness had been bait. When the shadow arrived carrying the eldest son's soul, she took it to her heart as her son at once and drove away the younger one who had come home hoping to hold her. The one who stepped out at dawn wore the younger son's face — but called out 'Mama' in the eldest son's voice.
hints: The mother's mistaking one son for the other was her own choice.
Inside the shadow was the soul of her other son.
The mother faked illness to lure her younger son into selling his shadow, trading his likeness to win back her dead eldest son.

title: The Empty Room
story: Every time I moved, I would set aside one spare empty room. My friends said every place I had lived was haunted; I didn't believe them. This time I deliberately rented just one room. At night the moving company called and asked why I had left myself behind in the old house.
answer: Each time the man moved, the old place kept a copy of himself holding the memories of that time. At first these copies had no bodies and could only lodge in the room their owner deliberately left empty; the spare empty room in each new home housed the double brought over from the last one. The man had always taken them for imaginary friends who had kept him company since childhood, and never believed in ghosts. This time he refused to leave a room, breaking the arrangement that had kept his doubles bodiless; the newest double took on a body of its own and stayed behind in the old house, packing his things. The movers saw it there, then heard the man on the phone already at the new address — the same person in two places — and called to check.
hints: What each home left behind held his memories of that time.
The empty rooms were places kept for these doubles.
Once he refused to leave another room, the double gained a body — and the movers met another him in the old house.

title: The Reflection
story: In the last video my father sent, the clock tower stood upside down, yet he smiled and said he was safe. I turned the phone around, playing it over and over. Not until the toll of a bell near the end of the video did I understand: he had never left that tower.
answer: My father was trapped in a clock tower held by robbers. They forced him to record a video telling his family he was safe, with the camera allowed to show only him and nothing around him. The small window before him mirrored the pool below the tower, so the phone had captured the tower's reflection in the water — hence the clock tower upside down. The robbers took the background for an ordinary stretch of water and let the video go out. When the hour struck, the phone recorded an enormous bell sound from very close by, and his instinctive flinch — proof he was still beside the bell. His daughter recognized the familiar shape of the tower's crown in the pool, gave the video to the rescuers who were still searching for him, and stopped them from pulling out on the strength of the false message.
hints: What the camera caught was a reflection in the water.
The words of reassurance were spoken under duress.
The reflection and the bell tolling inches away proved her father was still trapped in the tower.

title: The Best Seat in the House
story: The most expensive seat in the theater happened to be hidden behind a pillar. I was attending to the boss's honored guest, and all evening I never saw him move. After the curtain fell I went over to call him — and found his hands nailed to the armrests. The actors on stage had known he was there all along.
answer: The honored guest was a tyrant who controlled the troupe and had once beaten an actress to death for refusing him. Several members of the troupe plotted their revenge: they killed him before the show, propped the body in the seat of honor hidden behind the pillar, and staged him as a spectator. The owner assigned the new hand, who knew nothing, to serve tea and bear witness — so that others would believe the tyrant had been alive through the whole performance, while every one of the plotters was on stage. Blocked by the pillar, the boy could see only the edge of a coat, and took the man for someone who disliked being disturbed. Only at the end, up close, did he see the marks that fixed the hands to the armrests and the body already cold — and realize he too had been cast in that 'performance'.
hints: A seat hidden by a pillar is perfect for faking someone's presence.
The actors had already taken their revenge before the curtain rose.
The body was propped upright in its seat, and the new hand was used to prove the guest had watched the whole show.

title: The Third Day
story: When the rescue team found us, my brother had not moved for three days. I said he was only asleep and begged them to carry him out first. The team leader lifted the blanket — and picked me up instead. One of my brother's hands stayed wedged in the gap behind me.
answer: After the earthquake, the brother and sister lay trapped under a collapsed floor slab. The brother saw that a loose chunk of slab could crush his sister at any moment, so he braced it with his hand and shoulder, holding open a little space. Wounded, he gradually lost consciousness and finally died, his body staying wedged exactly where it was. His little sister, too young to know what death meant, kept believing he was asleep. Lifting the blanket, the rescue leader took in the brother's posture and knew that moving him first would bring the slab down. The team shored up the debris, carried the girl out, and only then lifted the brother from the gap he had held to the end.
hints: The brother's body held up the unstable debris beside his sister.
Moving the brother first would have crushed the sister.
The brother was dead, yet his body was still protecting her; the rescuers had to save the living first.

title: Cut the Sound
story: Before our horror film opened, a woman called me. She begged me to cut the scream near the end — she said it was her daughter. I told her the sound had been bought from a stock library. She was quiet for a moment, then asked, 'Is there a triple knock at a door after it?'
answer: The woman's daughter had once been kidnapped. In the ransom recording the kidnappers mailed, the girl's scream was followed at once by three heavy knocks on a door — the accomplices' agreed signal to move the hostage. She never found her daughter, but she never forgot that sound. The film's sound effects were being sold anonymously by one of the kidnappers himself; he had cut out all the speech, sure no one could recognize it. The sound editor pulled up the original file and found the same three knocks after the scream, and a pet name not fully trimmed away. The mother listened and confirmed it was the same recording; following the account details left by the sale, the police reopened the missing-person case.
hints: The woman had heard this recording during her daughter's kidnapping.
The scream and the three knocks that follow belong to one old piece of live audio.
A kidnapper cut the ransom recording into a horror sound effect for sale; the mother recognized its unique sequence of sounds.

title: The Borrowing Record
story: In the library there is a book that records the whole life of whoever borrows it. I turned to the last page and found that thirty years from now I would die at this very table. I fled the city that night. Thirty years later, I came back of my own accord and reached my hand out to the young me across the table.
answer: The library makes a reader's first borrowing and last borrowing occupy the same moment. The young man read his death for the first time, fled in terror, and never saw clearly the old man across the table. Through thirty years of flight he married and had children, but the foreknowledge of his death never stopped tormenting him. Near the end, he read the librarian's note tucked behind the book and learned that the old man had been himself — and that at the first borrowing, a memory could be handed to the younger man. He returned to the appointed table, took his younger self's hand, and passed over every memory from those thirty years that made life worth living. The young man would still leave the city, and still walk toward that day — but at last he knew what would happen before the end.
hints: The first borrowing and the last one meet at this table.
The young man across the table is his own past self.
He came back to hand his younger self the memories worth living for, and ease the dread of those thirty years.

title: Second Earth
story: In an abandoned space station we found a shrunken Earth. A researcher parted the clouds and saw the roof of his own house torn open, his wife staring up at him. The captain ordered everyone to fall back at once. Yet at that same moment, the captain's voice came over the broadcast system, also telling us to fall back.
answer: The globe inside the station was an interface to their real world—anything done to its surface took effect at the matching real location. When the researcher parted the clouds, he accidentally knocked the roof off his own house. The captain realized they might be inside a model nested inside another model and ordered everyone back. At that very moment, another team on a station one level up had discovered this same globe and was watching the station they were in; that captain's voice carried down through an open comm channel. The so-called Second Earth could not be kept apart from them: even the station they were exploring was itself someone else's desktop model.
hints: Changes made to the little Earth take effect in their real world.
The voice on the broadcast comes from the level above, which is watching a model of its own.
They realize they too live inside a model, watched by the people of a larger world.

title: Three Wishes
story: I wished for my daughter to come back to life, and the genie said it could be done. When she opened her eyes, I made a second wish—that she would never again be afraid of me. She stared at me for a while, then reached out and put her arms around my neck. The genie smiled and asked whether I still wanted my third wish.
answer: The man had killed his daughter when she walked in on his crime, and later wanted her back. He had the genie revive her, only to find her trembling at the sight of him. The second wish erased her fear of her father while leaving her memories intact. Unafraid now, she dared to walk up to the man who had killed her, put her arms around his neck, and whisper in his ear that she was going to the police. He had assumed that removing her fear would bring back the old father-daughter closeness; what he got instead was a witness who remembered everything and would never again be silenced by his threats. The genie stood by, waiting to see what he would trade away for his final wish.
hints: The father is the one who killed his daughter.
The second wish erased her fear but kept her memories.
No longer afraid, the daughter finally dares to tell him to his face that she will report him.

title: The Homing Needle
story: My father gave me a compass and said it always pointed home. Following it, I found my missing brother, and a burial ground without a single headstone. Back home, I pressed the compass into my father's hands. The moment he took it, the needle swung around and pointed at my chest.
answer: Once bound to an owner with a drop of blood, the compass points only to the person that owner killed with his own hands and who has not yet found rest. The father had secretly bound the compass with his own blood, then handed it to his younger son, claiming it pointed home, so the boy would recover the bones of the eldest son from the wasteland in his place. He had agreed with the village sorcerer that the wronged spirit would be sealed away once a family member brought the bones back—but he dared not go near the grave himself. After the younger son dug his brother up, the brother's spirit clung to him for a while and came home with him. When the father took the compass, the needle went on tracking the son he had killed, and so pointed at the younger brother's chest. Through the younger brother's mouth, the elder son called out "Father"—he had recognized the man who finally consented to take the compass.
hints: Before giving the compass away, the father bound it to himself with his own blood.
It tracks the ghost of the person its owner killed.
The elder brother's spirit rode the younger brother home, and the needle turned from the grave to the younger brother.

title: The Rain Never Stopped
story: It has rained on this city for seventeen years. The rain began the day I was born, and every evening my father went down to the river to wait for someone. Today, for the first time, he did not go. The rain has stopped—and from beneath the threshold of every house, a hand is reaching out.
answer: Seventeen years ago, a flood destroyed the villages at the city's edge. The city folk shut the floodgates to save their own district and left the fleeing villagers outside the walls. The father was one of the few who opened his door; he carried home a newborn—the narrator. When the drowned dead prepared to enter the city for revenge, the father struck a bargain with the river god: he would go to the river every night and call the roll of the dead, and in exchange the rain would keep falling, holding a curtain of water before the city gates and every threshold to bar the ghosts. Seventeen years later the father died of illness, and the final roll call was never finished. The rain stopped, the water curtain fell away, and the dead who had been turned away at the door finally crawled in through the very houses they had once begged for help.
hints: The rain is holding up a pact connected to the flood seventeen years ago.
The father went to the river each night to call the roll of the dead, one by one.
The pact broke when the father died, and the ghosts once shut out began entering the city for revenge.

title: The Last Line
story: A curse was laid on the village: whoever hears the nursery rhyme all the way through will die. I hunted the old woman who kept singing it for half my life, and I finally caught her. Again and again she called me by my childhood name, begging me to hear the last line. I covered her mouth and went home—to find my daughter humming the song as she rocked the crib.
answer: The rhyme attaches itself to a single line of mothers and daughters. The singer suffers no harm from her own song; anyone else who hears it through to the end dies that same day. If the singer is killed by an outsider, the curse skips a generation and passes to her granddaughter. It ends only if the singer lets her own child hear the rhyme in full and, in the last line, calls that child's childhood name—then the curse dies away together with mother and child. The old woman was the man's mother, separated from him in childhood. Driven by the curse to sing without stopping, she had recognized her son and hoped to end the bloodline's misfortune through him. Knowing nothing of his origins, the man gagged her and handed her to the villagers, who put her to death. The curse skipped over him and passed to the daughter in his house.
hints: After a singer dies, the rhyme reappears in the memory of one particular relative.
The old woman is the hunter's mother.
Killing the old woman passed the curse to his daughter; the singing at home means the next round has begun.

title: Bonfire
story: A blizzard sealed off the mountain, and we broke up the cabin's furniture to feed the fire. When the guide came back and saw half a bed board in the flames, he suddenly shoved me out the door. Only one bed was left in the cabin, and he set that one alight too, sat down on it, and never moved again.
answer: Years before, the guide had been trapped in that same cabin with a companion. To keep the food for himself, he killed the man and buried the body in a cavity under the bed, covering it with a bed board he had carved with the date and the man's name; after that he always avoided this cabin. Years later, leading tourists, he was caught by another blizzard and had no choice but to shelter here. The tourists knew nothing and tore one of the beds apart for firewood. In the firelight the old carving came to light, and the scattered bones were pushed aside as rotten wood. The guide knew the secret was about to surface: he shoved the narrator out into the snow and sent him to the nearby ranger station for help, then stayed behind in the burning cabin, meaning to burn the old crime away along with the remains. The tourist survived the snow—and remembered the name on that bed board.
hints: The guide had been through another blizzard in this same cabin.
The cavity under the bed held a body from years ago.
The old carving surfacing in the fire exposed the guide's murder of his companion; he meant to destroy the evidence along with himself and the cabin.

title: The White Line
story: After our son fell from the building, I kept the coat he last wore. Every time my wife saw the white line on the cuff, she cried. Later I went up to repaint the rooftop railing, and my wife followed. When she saw the paint can, she seized me and demanded to know who let go first that day.
answer: The father had abused his son for years. That night he dragged the boy to the rooftop and threatened to throw him off. The boy clutched the railing, and his cuff scraped against white paint that had been freshly brushed on. The father tore his hands free, and the boy fell—but the father told his wife the boy had jumped on his own, and that he had only just managed to catch hold of the coat. The wife had always taken the white line for a smear rubbed off the wall as he tried to save the boy. On the day of the repainting she found that the same white paint covered only the inner crossbar of the railing—the outer side and the wall were grey—while the paint on the cuff sat on the face turned toward the boy's palm, the inner side. Combined with what the boy had revealed about the abuse while he was alive, she pressed her husband until he admitted it: their son had been gripping the railing for his life.
hints: The white line came from fresh paint on the inner side of the railing.
The father says the boy jumped of his own will, but the mark matches a hand clamped hard on the railing.
The son was fighting to stay alive; the father tore his hands off, then claimed he had tried to save him.

title: One-Way Ticket
story: The train stopped on open wasteland, and the attendants began collecting tickets. I hid mine in my mouth and pretended I had lost it long ago. They put me off the train, and I knelt down and thanked them. After the train pulled away, I spat out the ticket; printed on the back was a small red X.
answer: During the war, a gang ran what looked like a refugee evacuation, selling those fit for hard labor to a secret mine. At the intake point, the chosen ones were given tickets marked with a red X on the back; en route the crew collected the tickets and locked those passengers alone into freight cars. At the previous station the narrator had watched red-X ticket holders being taken away bound, and he knew he had been chosen too. He hid his ticket and lied that he had slipped aboard to look for relatives. The attendants took him for a man who had never been selected; and since he also feigned weakness, they had no wish to feed him an extra ration and put him off. The wasteland was dangerous, but he counted himself lucky to have kept his freedom—and kept the ticket as evidence for reporting the whole transport line.
hints: The red X on the tickets marks the people who have been chosen.
He had already watched holders of the same ticket being taken away at the previous station.
The train was hauling forced laborers to a secret mine; hiding the ticket got him thrown off as a useless stowaway.

title: Someone in the Lantern
story: A lantern drifted in from the open sea, and someone inside it was crying for help. I fished it aboard, and the flame instantly became my wife's face. With one stroke the captain cut off my hand and threw it, lantern and all, back into the sea. I was still cursing him when my own cry for help rose from under the water.
answer: The sea demon used the lantern as a lure: whoever touched it saw the face he longed for most, and then his voice and body were dragged bit by bit down to the seabed. The captain had lost a whole ship's worth of companions in his youth; he recognized the lantern for what it was and at once cut off the hand the light had fastened onto, severing the bond before the devouring could spread. The demon got no more than the hand, but it had already learned the man's voice, and it went on calling for help in that voice. Only when he heard his own cry rising from under the water did the man understand what the captain had just prevented. The wife in the lantern had never truly come near the ship at all.
hints: The lantern uses the face a man misses most to make him refuse to let go.
The captain had seen this thing before; contact had to be cut off in time.
The demon takes voice and body through touch; the hand thrown into the sea let it learn his voice.

title: The Weight Limit
story: The escape pod could carry no more than two hundred kilograms. We threw out every piece of luggage, and the scale still read over the limit. I took off my helmet, and the ship's doctor lunged at me and clamped his hand over my mouth. The headcount on the pod door changed from three to four.
answer: An alien parasite could compress its body and hide in a human throat; its mass stayed unchanged, but the scanning system counted it and its host as a single person. The three crew members together weighed just under two hundred kilograms—with the parasite added, they were over the limit. The ship's doctor had found the infection during earlier examinations, but his unauthorized clearance had left him exposed to threats, so he meant to hide it until after the return and deal with it then. When the host took off his helmet, the parasite pushed a feeler out through his mouth, and for the first time the system recognized it as a separate living being: a fourth occupant. The doctor rushed to cover the mouth and push the feeler back in—but the weight that kept coming up over the limit had already been matched to the extra headcount.
hints: The extra weight comes from a hidden living thing.
The doctor had known about the infection all along and wanted to keep the system from recognizing it.
The parasite hides in the throat; only when it reached out through the mouth was it counted on its own.

title: The Sleeper
story: I woke from the hibernation pod, and my crewmates had all gone grey. They threw me a birthday party, with a single candle on the cake. I laughed and told them they had miscounted. The captain brought out a group photo from yesterday: in my place lay a white-haired old man with my own face.
answer: The ship had taken decades to reach its destination, and the crew had grown old together on the way. The narrator had been fatally wounded during the final repair spacewalk. The medical system could not save the original body, but with the cells and memories stored at launch it could rebuild a young version of him. The rebuilt man remembered only the time before launch; waking in the hibernation pod, he naturally assumed he had slept through one stretch of the voyage. The body that had truly lived those decades had died yesterday. His crewmates put a single candle on the cake for his new life, but he remembered nothing of the years they had shared. The captain brought out the last group photo and told him: the life that old man had lived through yesterday had also been his.
hints: His memories stop before launch, while his crewmates have lived together for decades.
The man who died yesterday and the man here now share the same pre-launch body and memories.
After the original body died, the medical system rebuilt him from young cells and old memories.

title: The Second Wedding Ring
story: After my husband died, I found two identical wedding rings under my pillow. I slid both onto my left hand, remembering how he had promised to come back and see me. At midnight, two husbands stood outside the door. Each held out a bare left hand, and each swore the other was the fake.
answer: The husband had secretly bought two soul-binding rings, wanting a spare chance at resurrection. Each ring held its owner's final body and memories; after his death, if the ring was put on by someone who loved him, it would rebuild him beside his grave, complete with those memories. He had worn one ring and taken it off on his deathbed, leaving it together with the spare one under the pillow. Not knowing how they worked, the wife put both rings on at once, and both resurrections happened at the same time. The two husbands who walked home each remembered buying the rings, the wedding, and his own dying, and each was certain the other had stolen his place. The true body still lay in the grave: the resurrections granted by the two rings had both come true at once.
hints: Each ring held the same man's body and memories.
After the owner's death, a loved one putting on the ring triggers one rebuilding.
She put on both at once and brought back two men who each remembered being the husband.

title: Your Voice, Sold
story: At an auction, someone raised a paddle and bought my voice. I thought I would never speak again. Back home, everything worked as usual—until the day of the trial, when I took the witness stand and heard my own mouth make the murderer's excuses.
answer: What the auction house sold was the use of the voice, effective only for a single occasion the buyer named in advance. The murderer's family had bought the witness's right to speak at this trial. It left his everyday speech untouched, so he had taken the auction for a swindle. In court he meant to describe the murder he had seen with his own eyes, but his voice spoke, word for word, the testimony the buyer had written. His body still obeyed him: he shook his head again and again and wrote the opposite facts on paper, and only then did the court see that his mouth and his will were coming apart. The buyer owned the voice of the testimony; his hands could not be bought along with it.
hints: The sale takes effect only for the one speech the buyer designated.
The words he says in court come from a script someone else wrote in advance.
The murderer's side bought the voice of his testimony, but the witness can still expose the truth in writing.

title: The Edge of the Map
story: The city's streets change every day, so all we can go by are the maps the mayor hands out. My brother drew a bridge at the edge of his map, and the next day he vanished. I walked outward along the bridge he had drawn—and for the first time, I saw someone raise an eraser into the sky.
answer: The whole city existed on a living map that could be redrawn: roads drawn on the map appeared, and whatever was erased vanished, people along with it. The mayor was a puppet set up by the wardens outside, in charge of issuing partial maps so the residents would keep circling inside the city. The brother discovered that his sheet was a proof copy able to affect the original; he drew a bridge at its edge, trying to reach beyond the paper. Once he touched the border, the wardens erased him. Following the bridge he drew, the sister walked to the outer rim and saw a giant human hand holding an eraser aloft; she understood at last that his disappearance and the shifting streets came from the same force, and that the whole city's only exit lay at the tear in the paper.
hints: The map directly changes the city.
The brother drew a bridge leading off the map.
The city is drawn on paper by people outside; the missing and the roads alike can be erased away together.

title: Please Knock
story: Deep in the mountains there is a wooden hut, and the person inside begged me to let him out. I pulled the nails from the door, but he said that was not enough. At his request, I knocked three times. The inside fell silent—and the same three knocks sounded behind me, while the voice inside the hut had become mine.
answer: The hut held a ghost that trades places with its visitors. The nails in the door only kept bodies from passing in and out; the true seal was the boundary between inside and outside: whoever stood outside and knocked three times of his own accord would swap places with the prisoner within. The ghost pretended to be a passerby trapped by the nailed-shut door—first it had the visitor pull the nails, then, pleading that the latch would not open, asked him to knock as a signal. As the third knock fell, the visitor stood inside the hut and the ghost stood behind him, in the visitor's old place. The ghost mimicked his knocking and took the nails away from outside the door; the cries for help coming from the hut belonged to the man who had just found himself shut in.
hints: The nails and the seal that truly holds the ghost are two different things.
Knocking three times of your own accord swaps the person outside with the one inside.
The one inside talked him into completing the swap, walked out, and left the new pleader locked in the hut.

title: Before It Melts
story: The wax museum's cooling system broke down, and the curator had us carry out the most lifelike figure first. The van was warm, and the wax face began to slide downward. The face I saw beneath it was identical to the one above. Through the van door, the curator asked, "Has it melted?"
answer: The curator had killed his partner, who was demanding his share of the take, coated the body in a thin layer of wax, and hidden it among the life-sized figures, relying on the cooling to keep it cold until it could be moved. The partner had been the living model for that very figure, so the surface face matched the face underneath. When the cooling failed, he was in a hurry to move the body elsewhere, but ordered only "the most lifelike one" carried out, to avoid giving away what it was. As the van warmed up, the thin wax softened and peeled away first, baring real skin and real wounds. The curator asked whether it had melted because he feared the disguise had already come off; and the movers, for the first time, knew what they had carried out of the exhibition hall.
hints: This figure was modeled on a real person.
The wax on the surface is thin; there is another face beneath it, a real one.
The curator hid his partner's wax-coated body among the exhibits, and the cooling failure forced him to move it.

title: The Name on the Gift
story: Before my father disappeared, he mailed me a cloth teddy bear. My mother told me to throw away the wrapping, but I had seen that the sender's name had been crossed out three times. Years later, a man came to our house with a gift and wrote my mother a card. The moment I saw his handwriting, I grabbed the teddy bear and ran.
answer: The father had found out that his wife and her accomplice were plotting to take his assets, and was preparing to leave with his daughter; the accomplice murdered him before they set out. To delay discovery, the killer mailed out the girl's birthday present using the shipping label the father had already filled in. Writing in the sender, he put down his own name out of habit, struck it out, and wrote the father's name in its place—leaving his distinctive cursive and the marks of the corrections. The daughter kept the wrapping and hid it inside the teddy bear's clothes. Years later, when her mother's new partner came to visit, the name and the cursive on his card brought that old shipping label back to her mind. She grabbed the bear and ran: she meant to take both pieces of handwriting to the aunt who had never stopped looking into her father's disappearance.
hints: The gift was mailed by someone else, after the father was killed.
The wrong name and the handwriting on the shipping label were kept all along.
The visitor's handwriting on the card gave away his link to that last gift; the old wrapping was hidden inside the teddy bear.

title: The Last Name
story: On the expedition roster, the last line was always blank. The leader said it was reserved for whoever would save us. Five days later, only two of us were left, and he finally wrote my name on that line. I looked at the ropes left in his pack and slipped out of camp that same night.
answer: The leader had been hired to guide the team to a cache buried during the war, and before setting out he had lied that he had filed their route with the outside world. Along the way he sent members out to scout separately, and one after another they never came back; in truth he wanted the find to himself and was using the deadly terrain to kill them off. The roster was meant to be forged into a farewell note at the end: the last line was for a scapegoat who would take the blame for the accident and be said to have stayed behind to save the others. With only the narrator left, the leader filled in his name, planning to post him at the foot of a cliff the next day and then cut the rope. The narrator had already seen several lengths of old rope in the leader's pack, every cut far too clean, and now watched the roster being rewritten; he finally understood how the others' disappearances were tied to the blank line "for our rescuer."
hints: The missing members' ropes were back in the leader's pack, their cut ends far too neat.
The roster was meant to explain the other members' deaths.
The leader wanted the find to himself and cast the last survivor as the scapegoat of a fatal accident.

title: A Hundred Calls for Help
story: On the beach I picked up a hundred drift bottles; the letters inside them were all in the same hand, signed with the same name. When I found the writer, he was drinking tea in his courtyard. He read the first letter and immediately locked the courtyard gate. The next day, the ground outside was covered with bare footprints, every left foot missing the same toe.
answer: Marooned on a desert island, the man had used a device on the island to make a hundred copies of himself to search for a way out, and each copy had sealed a letter calling for rescue into the sea. Later they found only one small boat that could carry a single person, and a hundred and one men, in fear and suspicion, began to kill one another. The one who survived to the end was the original, and he left the island alone. The dead men's spirits settled into the letters they had left behind; on the back of each sheet surfaced the story of how that one had been killed. When the bottle-picker brought the bottles round, the survivor read the details of one murder he had committed with his own hands, and knew the others had come back as well. In the night, the dead followed their one shared memory to the same house; every one of them carried the man's boyhood injury to the left foot, and every one of them felt the living man inside had taken his place.
hints: The identical handwriting belongs to many copies of the same man.
They killed one another over the chance to leave the island, until only one survivor was left.
The dead returned with their letters for help; each remembers the same home and bears the same injured foot.

title: Keep It Down
story: After my wife was gone, I bought a bottle that could pack sounds away. Whenever I heard crying in the night, I pulled the stopper. After a few years, the building was finally quiet. On moving day the bottle broke—and the neighbors opened their doors one after another, calling their children's names.
answer: Any sound the bottle drew in dragged the speaker's soul in with it. The man's wife had died in an apartment fire that also took several children. The surviving neighbors often heard a child crying in the night and put it down to their own grieving. Not knowing what the bottle truly was, the man first packed away his wife's crying, then little by little the voices of the other dead in the building, and everyone believed the trauma had finally gone quiet. When the bottle shattered, the dead were freed: each followed the door in their memory back home, and the children's voices sounded again outside their parents' doors. The last thing the man heard was his wife asking why he had shut her away for so long.
hints: The sounds the bottle took away belonged to the dead of the fire.
When a sound is taken, the soul that made it is trapped too.
The broken bottle freed the dead; they went back to their own doors and woke the people still longing for them.

title: Shared Bread
story: On the wasteland, an old man gave us a loaf of bread that could never be finished. Every piece we broke off grew back. On it we walked out of the desert. When I got home, I found my mother worn down to skin and bone—and a loaf of bread at her bedside.
answer: The old man sold bread in linked pairs: whenever one loaf was eaten, an equal weight of flesh and blood was drawn from the holder of the other to restore it. Hearing her son was missing on the wasteland, the mother had paid with her own body and asked the old man to put the life-sustaining loaf into her son's hands. She kept the paired loaf herself, never daring to pass it to anyone else and let a stranger suffer in her place. Son and companions, not knowing where it came from, shared it for many days and finally walked out of the desert; each time he calmly broke off another piece, his mother at home paid with a piece of herself. When the son came home, the loaf at her bedside was still whole.
hints: The two loaves are bound by a fixed exchange.
The cost of restoring the eaten bread falls on the holder of the other loaf.
The mother fed her son with her own body, and she paid for every piece he shared with his companions as well.

title: The Polar Night Greenhouse
story: On the sixtieth day of polar night, every flower in the greenhouse had turned to bloom downward, into the soil. We dug up the earth and uncovered a closed eye. The station chief told everyone to stand back—then turned on every light there was. The eye narrowed, and the distant iceberg began to move.
answer: The research station stood on the ice-covered back of a sleeping colossus. A crack in the floor at the corner of the greenhouse had always given off a faint warm glow; the researchers took it for old equipment buried underground, and all through the polar night the plants leaned toward that corner. Only after peeling back the thin soil and the ice crust did they see that the light came from the rim of the creature's eyelid. The station chief had seen a vast, symmetrical shape beneath the ice on the survey charts, and only now understood what it was; he ordered everyone out of the dug-open area at once. He threw on the floodlights, hoping the glare would drive the eye to close again and buy time to evacuate. The eye did narrow—but the thing was already waking, and far off, the shoulder everyone had mistaken for an iceberg lifted with its stirring.
hints: The greenhouse plants were chasing a point of light coming from underground.
The glowing thing beneath the ice belongs to an enormous living creature.
The station and the distant iceberg both sit on the colossus's back; with the eye uncovered, it is waking up.

title: Exact Change
story: By a grave I picked up seven copper coins, and after I spent them they came back to me every day. At first I was delighted. On the seventh day the money did not come back; instead, the seven people I had bought things from were standing together outside my door. They said it was my turn to give change.
answer: The seven copper coins were spirit money, the dead man's pay for hired pallbearers. Each time the finder spent one, he assigned whoever took it a night's service carrying the coffin for the grave's owner; the next day the coin returned to the finder's hand, while the one who had taken it lost part of his lifespan. For six days the man kept spending them over and over, passing the duty on to seven shopkeepers he knew. On the seventh night, the grave's owner gathered all the coins back and allowed the men who had been used to come and take back their years. The total the seven could reclaim was exactly the debt the man had run up in their names. He had assumed the coins would keep coming back forever; it never crossed his mind that the debt was recorded under his own name.
hints: The coins were originally payment for pallbearers.
Spending a coin hands a life-draining errand to whoever receives it.
Once the seventh night ends, the victims can claim back their stolen years from the man who picked up the coins.

title: The Fourth Crewman
story: The return capsule had only three seats, but the life-signs detector read four people. We searched every corner and found nothing. As we drew close to Earth, I saw four faces reflected in the porthole. The fourth face had been hiding behind my own the whole time.
answer: An alien civilization had pressed the consciousness of another astronaut into his nervous system, using him as its ferry back to Earth. Two minds shared one body, so there were always only three bodies aboard, while the life-signs detector counted separate minds and read four crewmen. The porthole's special light-sensitive layer was built to display states of consciousness; nearing Earth it was triggered by the ground scan, and the lodger's face was superimposed on the glass. The fourth was a crewmate lost during the mission, his memories already taken over by the alien civilization. He had hidden inside his companion's skull all along, waiting for the return to seize the body—the humans themselves had carried it into their home.
hints: The detector counts separate minds; there are only three bodies in the capsule.
A crewmate went missing during the mission.
A fourth consciousness lodges in his brain, riding the capsule back to deliver the alien that controls it to Earth.

title: The Last Watchman
story: My grandfather kept watch over that garden for sixty years without one whole night's sleep. After he died, I stood his first night shift. The flowers opened fast, one after another, and at the heart of each one was a familiar face. At daybreak the townspeople came to offer condolences—and every one of them knelt at my feet.
answer: The town had been destroyed by a disaster sixty years before. The grandfather had borrowed seeds from the thing underground: one seed grown into one flower could bring one of the dead back to live in the town. At night the flowers opened in turn, and before each one fully bloomed the keeper had to call out that dead person's name and fold the petals closed; otherwise the borrowed soul would be reclaimed from below. That was why he never dared sleep a whole night. After his death, his grandson took up the night log but nodded off from exhaustion; waking to the familiar faces at the hearts of the flowers, he hurried to fold the flowers one by one, reading the names. That night every townsperson dreamed of being back at the scene of the disaster; they knew the old watchman was dead, and they knew who had called them back in time. When they came to mourn at daybreak, they knelt and begged the grandson to take over the night watch his grandfather had never been released from.
hints: Every flower in the garden matches one person of the town.
The grandfather's years without sleep were what kept those people alive.
The whole town is made of borrowed dead; with the grandfather gone, they demand the grandson take up the night watch that allows no sleep.
